title: Fifteen to seventy
hook: at fifteen I set my heart on learning; at seventy I could follow my heart without going wrong (Analects 2.4)
tomorrow: a king tries everything under the sun to find what lasts. what's left?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two kinds of teacher: the worthy to equal, the unworthy to send you inward. Examine myself. Today Confucius turns that exam on his own whole life.

Asked to sum up your life so far, where would you even start? Confucius did it in six sentences, and they end with a heart he could finally trust. First, a scene. A lord, the Duke of She, asks Zilu what his teacher is like, and Zilu, for once, says nothing. Afterward Confucius tells him what he could have said: here is a man so eager to learn he forgets to eat, so glad in it he forgets his worries, and doesn't notice old age coming on.
screen: `A LIFE IN SIX SENTENCES.` → `ZILU SAYS NOTHING.` → `HE FORGETS TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Then the six sentences, Analects 2.4. At fifteen, he set his heart on learning. At thirty, he stood firm. At forty, no more doubts. At fifty, he knew what Heaven asked of him. Then the strangest line, in Legge: "At sixty, my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth." Not his eyes, not his mind: his ear. Some readers take it as hearing what's said, even the hard parts, without bristling. And the ending: "At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right." That's how it ends. The rules have become the heart, so wanting and doing right are one move. Here's the teaching, plainly. In the Confucian tradition, becoming a person is a lifelong craft, practiced decade by decade, and its summit isn't knowing more. It's a kind of freedom: the right way worn so deep it feels like your own wanting. Here's the surprise: Confucius puts listening at sixty, a decade after he says he knew Heaven's will. Even then, he still had to learn to hear.
screen: `FIFTEEN: A HEART SET ON LEARNING.` · `FIFTY: WHAT HEAVEN ASKS.` · `SIXTY: THE EAR.` · `SEVENTY: THE HEART CAN BE TRUSTED.` · then, large: `MY DECADES.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and paper and write your own decades in the shape of 2.4, one short line each, as far as you've lived, and one line for a decade you haven't reached yet. Then put the pen down and listen for the rest of the time: the room, the street, your own breath. That's the sense Confucius gave to sixty, and it can start now.
Fifteen to seventy: Confucius's life in six steps, from a heart set on learning to a heart that can be trusted.
Pocket this one: my decades, each with its own lesson, including the one you're in. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Analects take 2.4 as a map of lifelong self-cultivation, one stage for each decade, ending in a heart that has been trained until it can be trusted.

fork.setup: a friend says 'follow your heart' is the whole lesson of Analects 2.4. what's missing?
options: the decades before it: the heart is trustworthy at seventy because it was trained.
nothing: Confucius taught that the heart is right at any age.

fork.reveal: 2.4 ends with the free heart, but only after learning, standing firm, knowing Heaven's will and learning to listen.
